concept.name: Tightness
concept.definition: The cost dimension of market liquidity in the Sarr and Lybek (IMF, 2002) framework: the ability to trade at low transaction cost, conventionally measured by the narrowness of the bid-ask spread, which compensates liquidity providers for offering immediacy in executing buy and sell orders.
concept.intuition: It answers: how little do I lose by buying and immediately selling again - the tightness of the round trip.
concept.mechanics: Measured by quoted, effective, or realized spreads in absolute terms or relative to the quote midpoint; tighter markets feature smaller spreads for a given size, reflecting lower order-processing, inventory, and adverse-selection costs.
concept.formula: Relative tightness proxy: (A - B) / M, where A and B are the best ask and bid and M = (A + B) / 2.
concept.failure_modes: A tight spread for 100 shares says little about the cost of trading institutional size; minimum tick sizes can also artificially compress or mask the true economic spread.
concept.misconceptions: Tightness is not synonymous with overall liquidity - a market can be tight but shallow, so large orders still move the price substantially.
concept.example: A penny-wide spread on a $100 stock implies a round-trip quoted cost of about 1 basis point - a very tight market at small size.

citations.source: Sarr and Lybek, 'Measuring Liquidity in Financial Markets', IMF Working Paper WP/02/232
